content:
Ever feel like every pop song on the radio sounds the same? Or guess the ending of a horror film after just 20 minutes?

In a new paper published in Frontiers in Psychology, researchers from Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore argue that 'hyperselection' is occurring in highly competitive environments—where humans become increasingly skilled at identifying and optimising what works, continually filtering for the same traits rather than trying alternatives.

This is a major blow to creativity. In an increasingly optimised world, hyperselection could be making everything from music to urban planning to football matches more boring.

The study's lead author, research psychologist Jose C. Yong, likens hyperselection to natural selection—the evolutionary process whereby individuals with advantageous traits or more effective strategies are more likely to survive and reproduce. Modern technology has made this selection process exceptionally rapid and intense.

"We can now identify the best-performing option, replicate it almost immediately, and keep optimising it. When there is strong selection pressure, such as fierce competition or serious consequences for not optimising, this process accelerates," Yong said.

Optimisation is generally useful, as it helps us achieve our goals more efficiently. But when everyone optimises in the same direction, alternative traits, behaviours, products and strategies can disappear, resulting in 'a trade-off of efficiency at the cost of diversity or variation, which may actually be more adaptive and useful.'

When we fall into hyperselection, we miss out on creative masterpieces like 'Bohemian Rhapsody.'

When explaining the concept of hyperselection to audiences unfamiliar with it, Yong likes to use Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody' as an example. Released in 1975, the single was described by critics at the time as a 'bold pastiche' and a 'discordant hodgepodge of styles,' yet it is now regarded as one of the greatest songs in rock history—largely because the band was willing to take creative risks.

'Bohemian Rhapsody' is the opposite of hyperselection.

"The song is nearly six minutes long, spans wildly different musical sections, has no conventional verse-chorus structure, and famously features an operatic passage," Yong noted.

Another song that clearly does not fit hyperselection is Stevie Nicks's 'Edge of Seventeen,' whose unconventional song structure and distinctive sound make it instantly memorable. Yong also mentions System of a Down, whose music sounds 'outrageously weird' to him, yet still managed to chart—'precisely because it was so fresh and unique.'

Compared to the past, the songs dominating radio today often feel derivative and dull—so much so that even Yong struggles to pick one as an example.

"Honestly, I'm not sure I can single out a contemporary pop song as a typical example of hyperselection, partly because pop songs today all sound so similar that none really stand out," he admitted.

He also pointed out that certain music genres show clear signs of hyperselection, such as brooding, low-energy pop or the mumble rap that was ubiquitous a few years ago.

Hyperselection is also the reason Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan barely listens to the radio anymore, opting instead to discover lesser-known emerging indie artists.

"It's not that my taste has changed—it's that the world has changed. I crave rich, nuanced emotional expression, which today's pop music no longer provides," Tan told HuffPost.

Yong noted that, driven by streaming data, marketing considerations, and the fleeting attention spans of social media, the music industry has long shown a clear trend toward shorter songs and simpler arrangements—a phenomenon already well documented in the literature.

Beyond music, where else does hyperselection appear?

Yong, Tan, and their other co-author Simon S. Groome argued that the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency has made all aspects of our lives more predictable, formulaic, and boring—and this is also visible in sports.

In professional football, every team seeks tactics that give them an edge. When one strategy proves effective, opponents quickly follow suit. Matches become more intense and tactics more sophisticated, but teams' playing styles are also increasingly similar, leaving little room for individual expression.

The corporate world is no exception. Tan, drawing on his own background, discussed the situation in academia.

"When we were in graduate school, we were taught to think big, explore new ideas, and figure out how the world works," he said.

In an ideal world, the best researchers would be the most creative problem-solvers—those bold enough to be different. In reality, however, things are far from this ideal.

Tan pointed out: "When academia pressures researchers to prove their worth, what matters is no longer the value of their research ideas, but metrics like the number of publications, citation counts, and the amount of research funding raised."

He added: "The 'P' in PhD—Philosophy—has long become a dead letter. Once we see the same pattern repeatedly emerging in other areas of life, we can't help but ask whether some fundamental force is driving these trends."

AI will accelerate hyperselection

It almost goes without saying that AI will accelerate hyperselection. Yong pointed out that AI is designed to recursively self-optimise with little to no human intervention, operating at speeds and scales far beyond what humans or previous technologies could achieve.

"We're already starting to see this in online content—AI-generated articles, marketing copy, social media posts, images, videos, website designs, and even music all feel strikingly similar because they stem from the same underlying patterns and are continually optimised based on 'what works,'" he said.

If people accept this content unthinkingly, they will hardly provide any counterforce to AI-driven hyperselection.

Hyperselection is not entirely negative, but artists need to be aware of it.

Yong emphasised that optimisation itself is not a bad thing and can help people achieve goals and improve their lives. However, because the pressure to optimise is often extremely strong, artists may unknowingly sacrifice adaptive variation in the process.

"That's exactly why being aware of hyperselection is crucial, and it's part of why I want to clarify this concept—only by recognising it can we think about how to respond when it happens," he said.

Yong said the key lies in recognising how easily we fall into the trap of hyperselection, and finding ways to nurture creativity and defend diversity.

"Creativity often comes from encountering different things and combining them in new ways. If everything starts to look, sound, and function the same, we lose a treasure trove of alternative strategies, and we lose the raw material from which new ideas can sprout," he noted.

We also need to be more critical of the content we consume.

"If audiences can recognise when music, film, or other cultural products have become too formulaic and actively demand something more interesting, that alone will change the selection pressures acting on the production side," Yong said.
